entries.title: Tracking the flow of interstellar gas across scales: from galaxies to star clusters
entries.summary: While the baryon cycle of the interstellar medium - and its ability to form stars - plays a key role in galaxy evolution, unravelling the physical processes driving its evolution remains a critical challenge, given that present-day observing facilities are unable to map entire galactic ecosystems down to the scales of individual star-forming clumps. Here, we outline the technical requirements that would enable, for the first time, to connect the small (pc) scale physics of star formation, to the large (tens-of-kpc) scales of galaxies, enabling an effective tracking of the flows of matter and energy across a vast range of environments, and answering the long-standing question of what regulates star formation across cosmic time.
entries.arxiv:comment: Part of the ALMA2040 White Paper Series

entries.title: The optical colors of hidden spiral-like features in nine Virgo early--type dwarfs
entries.summary: Dwarf early-type galaxies (ETGs) are abundant in nearby clusters and provide a key laboratory for studying environmentally driven galaxy transformation. Although dwarf ETGs were once considered structurally simple, deep imaging has revealed embedded spiral-like features (e.g., bars and spiral arms) in some of them, contributing only a small fraction of the total light. Their origin at dwarf scales remains uncertain. As a pilot study, we investigate spiral-like features in nine Virgo dwarf ETGs with clear embedded arms, using optical colors to test whether these features differ from the surrounding diffuse component, which would constrain their formation pathways. Using deep g- and i-band NGVS images, we apply a residual-based method to separate excess light associated with the spiral-like component from the diffuse host. The residual images define arm and interarm regions, enabling direct measurements of light fractions and g-i colors for both components. The spiral-like features contribute only a few percent of the total light (about 1.5-5.5% in i and 1.7-3.7% in g). We find a diverse range of colors across the sample: four galaxies host spiral-like features redder than their interarm regions, four show no robust arm-interarm color difference, and one exhibits a distinctly bluer spiral-like component. The latter is consistent with a recently quenched transition object, while the redder and color-uniform features are consistent with older or more metal-rich stellar populations. Spiral-like features in Virgo dwarf ETGs thus exhibit a surprising diversity in their photometric properties, implying multiple evolutionary channels rather than a single one. This pilot analysis also demonstrates readiness for the much larger NGVS sample of dwarfs with potential spiral-like features.
entries.arxiv:comment: Accepted for publication in Astronomy and Astrophysics

entries.title: Anchoring the Chromospheric Activity$-$Rotation Relation: A Study of the Pleiades and Group X
entries.summary: We present a study of the rotation and the chromospheric H$α$ activity of low-mass stars in the $\approx$120 Myr-old Pleiades and the $\approx$400 Myr-old Group X open clusters. We combine published and new rotation periods ($P_\mathrm{rot}$) from TESS and ZTF, and use LAMOST, SDSS, and MDM spectra to measure H$α$ equivalent widths (EWs). While overall the Group X distributions of $P_\mathrm{rot}$ and EWs are as expected, detailed comparisons to the Pleiades and to the 700-Myr-old benchmark Praesepe produce some surprises. For F through mid K stars, the Group X color$-$period sequence lies between those of the Pleiades and of Praesepe, as expected. But the $P_\mathrm{rot}$ for its late K and early M dwarfs and the Praesepe slow-rotator sequence overlap, indicating that the 700 Myr-old stars have not spun down significantly despite being nearly twice as old as their Group X counterparts. In the Rossby number$-L_\mathrm{Hα}/L_\mathrm{bol}$ plane, rapid rotators in Group X are saturated, as is seen in older clusters, whereas the rapid rotators in the Pleiades show a weak but measurable dependence of $L_\mathrm{Hα}/L_\mathrm{bol}$ on rotation. This implies that the chromospheric activity$-$rotation relation attains its mature form between 120 and 400 Myr. Dividing the sample by color reveals that K, M0, and M1 dwarfs are no longer saturated by $\approx$120 Myr, M2 and M3 dwarfs become unsaturated between $\approx$400 and $\approx$700 Myr, and later M dwarfs remain largely saturated through field ages even as their saturated $L_\mathrm{Hα}/L_\mathrm{bol}$ levels decline, indicating that chromospheric evolution is not determined by rotation period alone.

entries.title: Atypical White Dwarfs in Open Clusters
entries.summary: Open clusters are powerful laboratories for investigating the formation and evolution of white dwarfs (WDs), as their well-constrained ages link WDs to their progenitor stars. This is particularly valuable for atypical WDs, including magnetic WDs and those with non-hydrogen-dominated spectra, whose origins can be difficult to disentangle in the field. We assemble the largest sample to date of atypical WDs in open clusters: eight non-magnetic WDs with helium-dominated spectra, five with featureless spectra, and five magnetic WDs showing hydrogen or helium lines. We find no significant difference between the initial--final mass relations of hydrogen- and helium-atmosphere WDs, nor robust spatial or kinematic differences. The strongest difference from the field is a deficit of non-DAs between $0.8$ and $1.0\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$, where the field predicts $6.0^{+0.8}_{-0.7}$ WDs, yet none are observed, with a probability of only $0.37\%$. Massive magnetic WDs show a similar deficit: only one of 20 cluster WDs with $M_{\mathrm{WD}}\geq1.0\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$ and $T_{\mathrm{eff}}\geq20{,}000\,{\rm K}$ is magnetic, compared with 10 of 16 in the field. Together, these deficits are consistent with an additional field population of massive merger remnants, particularly high-mass magnetic WDs and warm/hot DQs. Such objects may be underrepresented in clusters because young systems provide limited time for certain classes of delayed mergers, while older clusters lose members or dissolve; the field accumulates binary evolution products over Galactic timescales. Magnetic cluster WDs consistent with single-star evolution further suggest mass-dependent magnetic-field emergence, with fields appearing early in some massive WDs while young lower-mass WDs remain consistent with delayed emergence.

entries.title: A Multi-dimensional Analysis of the Open Clusters NGC 2423 and NGC 2482 with Gaia DR3
entries.summary: We present a homogeneous photometric, astrometric, and kinematic study of the Hyades-like open clusters NGC 2423 and NGC 2482 based on Gaia DR3 data. Cluster memberships are determined using the UPMASK algorithm in the multi-dimensional parameter space of (alpha, delta, parallax, mu_alpha cos(delta), mu_delta), with radial velocities incorporated when available. Gaussian modelling of the astrometric distributions yields mean trigonometric parallaxes of 1.060 +/- 0.035 mas and 0.735 +/- 0.061 mas, corresponding to astrometric distances of 944 +/- 31 pc and 1361 +/- 113 pc for NGC 2423 and NGC 2482, respectively. Fundamental parameters are derived through PARSEC isochrone fitting, resulting in ages of 1250 +/- 100 Myr and 445 +/- 50 Myr, observed distance moduli (m-M)_obs = 9.90 +/- 0.10 and 10.80 +/- 0.20 mag, and reddening values E(G_BP-G_RP) = 0.07 +/- 0.01 and 0.10 +/- 0.02 mag, equivalent to E(B-V) = 0.054 and 0.078. The corresponding photometric distances are 892 +/- 50 pc and 1311 +/- 146 pc. We further investigate the internal and global kinematics of both clusters using velocity-ellipsoid parameters, the convergent-point method, and action-angular-momentum diagnostics. The derived kinematic properties show that NGC 2482 closely matches the velocity-space characteristics of the Hyades stream, while NGC 2423 shares the characteristic rotational velocity and angular momentum of the Hyades-like population but is offset in its U component. Both clusters occupy the angular-momentum range associated in the literature with Hyades-like clusters and bar-related resonances, although this association is based on their present-day kinematics and action-space locations rather than a direct dynamical demonstration of resonance trapping.

entries.title: Quantifying the decline in CO(2-1) intensity around PHANGS-HST star clusters: Constraints on molecular gas dispersal, stellar feedback, and cluster formation efficiency
entries.summary: We combine the largest survey of star clusters in nearby galaxies to-date, PHANGS-HST, with maps of molecular gas maps from PHANGS-ALMA to constrain the efficiency of cluster formation and the typical timescales over which clusters become dis-associated from their natal molecular gas. We analyse 29,233 clusters in 36 galaxies using CO maps at 150 pc resolution. For each star cluster with stellar mass $\geq 10^{3.5}$ M$_\odot$, we measure the radial profiles of CO(2-1) integrated intensity and obtain local background-subtracted CO intensity, $I_{\rm CO}^{\rm bkgsub}$, at cluster centre. We group the clusters by age and mass to quantify the dependence of $I_{\rm CO}^{\rm bkgsub}$ and corresponding molecular gas mass, $M_{\rm mol}$, on these cluster properties. To account for the cluster mass ($M_{\rm SC}$) dependence, we also calculate the normalised mass ratio of $(M_{\rm mol}/M_{\rm SC})$. We find that CO intensity varies systematically with cluster age and mass. Clusters that are spatially associated with H$α$ emission exhibit the highest $I_{\rm CO}^{\rm bkgsub}$ of 7.4 K km s$^{-1}$, corresponding to a $M_{\rm mol}/M_{\rm SC}$ ratio of 82 and implying a cluster formation efficiency ($ε_{\rm obs}$) of $\sim 1.2\%$. Young clusters without associated H$α$ emission show lower and age-dependent $I_{\rm CO}^{\rm bkgsub}$ and $M_{\rm mol}/M_{\rm SC}$, decreasing from 1.3 K km s$^{-1}$ and 15 for clusters with age 1-3 Myr, to a level $\approx$ 0 for clusters older than 9--10 Myr. Clusters older than 10 Myr show no statistical excess of CO intensity. We use the clusters with H$α$ association as initial conditions to model the impact of cluster drift and demonstrate that this is unlikely to drive the observed cluster-gas spatial disassociation on short timescales of 4-6 Myr. Instead, early stellar feedback seems likely to be the main driver.
